title: The four churchwomen (1980)
hookLine: Maura Clarke, Ita Ford, Dorothy Kazel and Jean Donovan, killed in El Salvador

cards: Two of them have just flown back from a meeting in Nicaragua. The other two have driven out after dark to meet them at the airport outside San Salvador, in a white van.
Four American women: two Maryknoll sisters, an Ursuline sister and a young lay volunteer. They know the roads, the checkpoints, the risk. The van never reaches home.
Days later, local people point the way to a shallow grave by a country road. Their names were Maura Clarke, Ita Ford, Dorothy Kazel and Jean Donovan.

teach.b: It would be easy to tell this as a story about how they died. Their lives say more. First, who they were.
Maura Clarke and Ita Ford were Maryknoll sisters, members of an American Catholic missionary order. Dorothy Kazel was an Ursuline sister from Cleveland.
Jean Donovan wasn't a nun at all: she was a lay missionary, a young woman with a business career behind her, who had come to help. Second, what they did.

In a country at war, they drove refugees to safety, brought food and medicine to families hiding from the fighting, and helped bury the dead. Ordinary work, in a place where ordinary work had become dangerous.
Third, the choice to stay. Friends and family asked them to come home. Jean Donovan wrote that she had thought about leaving, but couldn't bring herself to abandon the children she cared for.
They knew what had happened to Romero.
They stayed with the poor. Fourth, the truth told.
Members of El Salvador's National Guard were later convicted of the killings, and questions about who gave the orders went on for years. Their families kept asking.

teach.h: BUT I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS.
teach.b: Some Catholics read their story beside the Last Supper in John's Gospel, where Jesus says he will no longer call his disciples servants, and then, in the Douay-Rheims: "But I have called you friends."
They hadn't gone to El Salvador to die. They went to be with people, and when staying became dangerous, they kept being with them.

how: Maryknoll, the Ursulines of Cleveland and parishes in El Salvador and the United States remember the four churchwomen with Masses and vigils, especially on the anniversary of their deaths.

practice: Picture someone far from home tonight because they chose to be with people who need help: a sister in a clinic, a volunteer at a border, a lay worker in a refugee camp, a doctor in a war zone.
Think what their day might hold, a long drive, a checkpoint, a child who needs medicine. If you pray, pray for missionaries and the people they stay with; if not, wish them safe roads.
